newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Jets fly, Mar durables in holding pattern.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Jets fly, Mar durables in holding pattern.

text.p: Soaring demand for aircraft may take some time to lift durable goods data again but robust industrial output probably prevented orders for big-ticket items from losing altitude in March, economists said.
March was one of the most fruitful months for U.S. industry in the last year, yielding a 0.9 percent jump in production. Experts said such frothy output often spills over into orders data.

"These days, with high technology industries, the lag between orders and shipments and production is very small, so you get a good indication from the industrial production report that things are still cooking," said Russell Sheldon, a senior economist at Mellon Bank Corp.

The normally volatile orders for durable goods were expected to be unchanged in March after soaring 1.5 percent to a record high $178.3 billion in February, according to forecasters polled by Reuters.
The durables data is due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Tuesday.

Transportation orders, led by civilian aircraft, are expected to recover somewhat, after sliding 3.6 percent and weighing on the overall number in February. That month, durable goods orders rose 3.1 percent when transport equipment was subtracted.

But analysts said it was a toss-up whether a rush of bookings reported by Boeing Co will show up in March or April. They also questioned if the surge in jet orders, which normally vary widely month-to-month, can be sustained.

"Aircraft orders of course have been a big item lately and those will be watched with care," said David Wyss, a research director at DRI/McGraw Hill. "No question Boeing is doing great but you just can't go up that much every month."
"Often they get distributed over months so it's not going to be as big the raw numbers," said Russell Sheldon, a senior economist at Mellon Bank Corp.
Data from auto manufactures should, on balance, have a positive bearing on durable goods in March, economists said.
But there are hints, more anecdotal than statistical, that weaker car production and sales could be a drag on orders data in the next month or two, economists said.

"If it's not in this month's report, it might be in the following month," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards and Sons Inc. "I don't know if (auto) manufacturers had concerns about that going into April or whether it would show up in the March number or not."

The heavy demand for long-lasting items in February was consistent with the potent U.S. economy. But if the pace of orders tapers off, it could foreshadow a moderation of growth in the second quarter, they said.
Economists also cautioned that the recent increase in interest rates and the expectations of more tightenings by the Federal Reserve this year might start to bite in March.

But given the see-saw nature of durable goods data, it does not tended to be a big item as far as Fed policy is concerned. Moreover, the number is likely to be submerged by a flood of other important data next week, economists said.

"The Fed is much more worried about the employment cost index (also Tuesday), about the GDP (gross domestic product) numbers out the next day and the employment number will be out that Friday," said Wyss. "It's sort of going to get drowned, because there are bigger numbers out the same week."
